h1: Choosing an Indian state for a brewery or distillery
title: Choosing an Indian State for a Plant | Craft Beer School
desc: How to choose an Indian state for a brewery or distillery: licensing, excise, raw materials, utilities, talent and where the product will sell.
teaser: In India the state you choose sets the rules for your business before you buy a single tank.
standfirst: Alcohol is a state subject in India, so the state you pick decides licences, taxes and routes to market. This guide gives a framework for comparing states with your advisers.
sections: Why the state matters so much

India has one central government and many state governments. Alcohol falls under the states. Each one sets its own licence types, excise duty, pricing, rules on brand and label registration and ways of selling. They differ and they change.

Several states, including Bihar and Gujarat, have prohibition. Others restrict sales or hours. Choosing a state is therefore the biggest early decision. Make it with a licensing adviser who works there.

• Licensing: what licences exist for a brewery or distillery, how long approvals take in practice and how stable the policy is
  • Excise and pricing: how the state taxes production and sale and how that affects your shelf price
  • Route to market: whether sales go through state outlets, private distributors, bars or direct sales
  • Where you can sell: whether you can sell in other states and on what terms
  • Raw materials: access to malt, grain, fruit or molasses and the cost of moving them
  • Water: quality and supply, since breweries and distilleries use a lot
  • Power and utilities: reliability and cost
  • Labour: skilled brewers, technicians and operators
  • Land and building rules: industrial zones, pollution control and local approvals
  • Incentives: any support for new industry, which varies and changes

Rank each factor by what matters for your plan. A distillery that needs grain wants a different state from a craft brewery that depends on a tourist or city market.

A plant must sit near the market it serves, or in a state that lets you ship to it. Moving beer or spirits across state lines usually involves licences and state duties. Check whether the state allows you to sell outside it.

Consumer demand is local too. Cities with a young, working population and a lively restaurant scene behave differently from small towns. Do market research in each state you are weighing. See market research in India for a foreign drinks brand.

Breweries and distilleries produce effluent and need approval from pollution control authorities. These approvals sit with the state boards and can take time. Ask your adviser what a given state expects, how it treats effluent from distilleries and whether the site you like can be approved.

Local rules on land use, building and fire safety add more steps. Check them before you buy land.

Pick three states. Score each factor from your own research and from what advisers tell you. Weight the factors. Do not average blindly: a state that scores high on everything except licensing may still be wrong, because a licence you cannot get is a project you cannot start.

Treat the result as a shortlist and then visit. Meet the licensing adviser, the possible landlord, the water supplier and a few local operators. The guide to cash flow forecasting and the note on funding a brewery help you test the finance in each shortlisted state.

The first mistake is choosing the state for a single attraction, such as cheap land. The buyer then discovers that the route to market is closed or slow. The second is relying on a policy that has just been announced. Policy can change before your plant is built, so look for stability as well as promise.

The third is copying another company's choice. Their product, partners and timing may differ from yours. Make your own comparison with your own numbers.

The fourth is skipping the visit. A week on the ground, meeting advisers, officials where appropriate and local operators, is cheap against a wrong decision.

Write down your reasons for the final choice, with the figures you used. When something changes, you can see which assumption broke and decide whether to move or hold.
faqs: Which state is best for a brewery?
There is no single answer. It depends on licensing, route to market, raw materials and your plan. Compare shortlisted states with an adviser.
Can I sell beer made in one state in another?
That depends on both states' rules and may involve extra licences. Check before you plan sales.
Yes. Policy, duty and licence terms change. Check the current notification each time.
